prime.problem: Ten cards of backward lines are easy to finish as 26 separate answers. Without the causal map that joins them, you can match autograd on this net yet be stuck on the next layer you meet, and unable to say why a gradient came out 0 or why cmp says False.
prime.fits: This is the front page of course 6, read first as the map or last as the recap. It takes micrograd's chain rule and += for reused nodes up to whole tensors, on the MLP with BatchNorm from the last two lectures. From the next course on, loss.backward() is back.
expect: dx = Σ over uses of (local gradient × upstream gradient), shaped like x
four rules: elementwise slope, broadcast → sum, sum → copy, reuse → +=
cmp against autograd: exact vs approximate
the short forms: (softmax − one-hot)/n and BatchNorm's one line
prime.goal: Draw the whole course as one causal map, from "autograd leaks" to "val 2.11 with no autograd", and for each lever (init, = vs +=, keepdim, n vs n − 1, atoms vs fused) say what it changes and the number it produced.

attend: The core formula has a Σ over uses. Which four tensors in Exercise 1 are the ones where that sum has two terms, and why is a broadcast a hidden version of the same sum?
Which card turns autograd from the thing you are replacing into the answer key you check against, and what trick makes a hidden bug show up?
Across the levers table, which mistakes produce an error message and which produce plausible numbers? What do the silent ones have in common?
Exercise 1 is bit-exact and Exercises 2–3 are only approximate. Where does that difference come from, and why is it not a bug?
Why can the last card switch autograd off entirely, and which two derivations had to happen on paper first for the backward pass to fit on one screen?

must: Autograd multiplies local gradients along every path → it is exact about the function you wrote, including a clipped loss or a saturated tanh with slope near 0 → a wrong function trains without crashing → knowing each op's local gradient is what lets you find where the gradient dies

Every d<name> must have <name>'s shape → a tensor used twice, or broadcast across rows, collects the sum of all its uses (+=, .sum(0), keepdim=True) → a forward sum hands the same gradient back to every input → four rules (slope, sum, copy, +=) write all 26 gradients

Autograd's .grad on 19 retained intermediates is an answer key → cmp checks each line as you write it, and random (not 0/1) inits stop a missing factor from hiding → a mistake is pinned to one line → exact means same arithmetic, approximate (~1e-9) means same math by a different route

Doing the calculus once on paper collapses long chains → cross-entropy becomes (softmax − one-hot)/n and BatchNorm one three-road line (dσ²/dμ = 0 drops a term) → the whole backward pass fits on one screen → loss.backward() can be deleted and the 12,297-parameter net still reaches val 2.1086
elevated: Matmul backward is two more matmuls with a transpose, picked by shape → each costs about as much as the forward multiply and no Jacobian is ever built → but when two dimensions are equal, a wrong order has the right shape, and only cmp catches it

BatchNorm's variance divides by n − 1 in this notebook → the backward line carries n/(n − 1), and nn.BatchNorm1d mixes ÷n (training) with ÷(n − 1) (running_var) → the same batch comes out with std 1.0000 in training and 0.9842 at test
reference: the chapter timestamps and the per-card numbers (loss 3.3444 on the lab's seed vs the video's 3.3377, 4,137 and 12,297 parameters)
Karpathy's variable names from logprobs back to emb

Put the ten cards as boxes in the order they are needed, draw an arrow for each because, and mark every place where a missing piece gives plausible numbers instead of an error.
checklist: autograd leaks → so write the backward pass once; chunk the forward pass and cmp each line against autograd (random inits so bugs show)
the softmax chain, sum ↔ broadcast, matmul by shapes, tanh and BatchNorm atoms, the embedding scatter-add: all four rules, 26 of 26 exact
Bessel's n − 1 as a side branch off BatchNorm's variance, feeding the one-liner's n/(n − 1)

retrieve.q: Explain to a programmer who has used loss.backward() but never looked inside it why this whole lecture reduces to one formula, dx = Σ over uses of local gradient × upstream gradient, and what the two hours add on top of it.
answer: the formula is micrograd's chain rule with +=, applied to tensors
on tensors, "uses" include every broadcast copy, so sums appear where the forward pass stretched a tensor
each op needs only its own local gradient: slope, transpose-matmul, copy, or sum
the two hours are the bookkeeping (shapes, second branches) and the checking (cmp), then the shortcuts derived on paper

retrieve.q: Walk one step of Exercise 4 from the loss back to C, naming the rule each backward line uses and the shape it produces.
answer: dlogits = (softmax − one-hot)/n, (32, 27)
dh, dW2 by matmul with a transpose, db2 by summing rows: (32, 200), (200, 27), (27,)
dhpreact = (1 − h²)·dh; dbngain, dbnbias sum over rows; dhprebn by the three-road line
dembcat, dW1, db1 by the same matmul rule; demb by viewing back to (32, 3, 10); dC by scatter-add with += for repeats
then every parameter moves by −lr × its gradient inside torch.no_grad()

retrieve.q: You have hand-written a backward pass for a new layer. Choose between checking it with cmp against autograd, with a numerical nudge, or by watching the training loss, and say what each can and can't tell you.
answer: cmp: exact per tensor with one backward call, pins the failing line; needs autograd to exist and random inits so 0/1 values don't hide a factor
numerical nudge: works with no autograd but costs two forward passes per number (8,274 for 4,137 parameters) and is only approximate
loss curve: cheapest, but a clipped loss or a missing branch can still train, so it says something is off, never where
approximate: True with maxdiff near 1e-9 is a pass for fused formulas; approximate: False is a bug

retrieve.q: Four half-finished lines print approximate: False in this course (counts, bndiff, hprebn, and C with fancy-index +=) while a missing max branch prints True. Why does one missing branch pass and the others fail?
answer: all five are a tensor whose second share of gradient was dropped
counts, bndiff and hprebn miss a real contribution: maxdiffs 0.00613, 0.00119, 0.000967
the dC[Xb] += version loses the repeated characters' extra rows: 0.0367
the max branch carries only float noise because the shift cancels in the softmax (1.02e-8), so it slips under allclose; it is still a missing branch

compare.q: The previous course's big idea was to look inside every layer (activations, gradients, update:data ≈ 1e-3) and to standardise preactivations with BatchNorm. This course writes those gradients by hand. What does knowing the backward lines add to the diagnostic plots, and where do the two courses meet?
answer: course 5 measures gradients autograd produced; course 6 knows the formula for each, so a flat or dead region can be predicted from the code
saturated tanh: course 5 sees it in histograms; here it is the 1 − h² factor going to 0
BatchNorm: course 5 builds the forward pass and running stats; here its backward is three roads, and each input's gradient depends on the whole batch
they meet at train/test: course 5's running statistics, and here Bessel's ÷n vs ÷(n − 1) mismatch inside them

compare.q: micrograd's overview had one formula, p ← p − lr · ∂L/∂p, with a scalar engine computing ∂L/∂p. This course keeps the update and throws the engine away. What replaces each part of micrograd's machinery, and what new failure appears only with tensors?
answer: Value objects and closures → one hand-written line per tensor op, in reverse order written by you
the += in _backward → += for reused tensors plus sums over broadcast axes
micrograd vs PyTorch check → cmp per tensor, exact and approximate
new with tensors: shape bugs that don't crash (a dropped keepdim, fancy-index += overwriting repeats, a square matmul in the wrong order)

predict.q: The next lecture goes back to the Part 3 code: 12k parameters, 3 characters of context, val 2.105. It wants a much lower loss. Commit before you look: does it keep hand-written backward passes, what does it change about the network, and will the result land above or below 2.0?
predict.answer: It brings loss.backward() back and packages the layers as torch.nn-style modules (Embedding, FlattenConsecutive, Sequential), because the aim now is architecture, not gradients. It widens the context from 3 to 8 characters and fuses it gradually in a tree (the WaveNet idea) instead of crushing it into one hidden layer. The notebook ends at 76,579 parameters, train 1.7690 / val 1.9937: below 2.0. On the way it hits a BatchNorm1d bug with 3-D inputs, where knowing which axis BatchNorm sums over (this course's rows) is what finds it.

apply.task: Break it and debug it. From a blank cell under the chunked forward pass, write all 26 gradient lines of Exercise 1 using only the four rules, with a cmp after each. Replace the dC double loop with one index_add_ call. Then delete the second-branch += line of each two-branch tensor (counts, logits, bndiff, hprebn), one at a time, and before running each, predict what cmp prints for that tensor.
apply.done: All 26 lines print exact: True | maxdiff: 0.0 (the lab's --all: 26 of 26 exact), index_add_ matches the loop with max |loop − index_add_| = 0.0, and your predictions match the half-finished verdicts: counts 0.00613, bndiff 0.00119, hprebn 0.000967 (approximate False), while logits without its max branch still passes allclose at 1.02e-8.
apply.hint: If a tensor is False and the error is the same small amount across a whole row or column, you are missing a broadcast's sum or a second branch, not a local derivative. Check that every reduction has keepdim=True where the variable is (32, 1) or (1, 64).
